title: Warm standby DNS & multi-region traffic shift notes
content:
Context:

This is a working draft capturing SRE on-call observations, lightweight post-incident notes, and a proposed runbook for region-level failures (partial/complete region outage, region-network partition, or severe capacity degradation requiring traffic shift). Focus areas: DNS behaviour, TTL/propagation realities, warm-standby prep, traffic-shifting mechanics (weights, gradual canary), and verification steps.

Summary of recent incidents (short):
- 2025-09-18: APAC region API pods OOM after a model rollout; autoscaler misconfigured -> 18 minutes degraded traffic; edge health checks failed and traffic routed to US-west but DNS weights were zero for fallback for one route. Human routing via GSLB fixed in 7 minutes once SRE changed weights manually.
- 2025-10-30: Network flap at cloud provider caused BGP-level loss for eu-west regional fabric; warm-standby instances in eu-central were ready but DNS TTLs (60s on Route53) and Cloudflare cache prevented full shift for ~4 minutes. Ground truth: application-level failover was fine, but client-level caching (CDN, ISP) stretched recovery time.

Key takeaways from incidents:
- Route53 weight-only changes are fast internally, but external resolvers and CDNs cause effective delay. We must treat DNS as an eventual consistency surface, not an instant switch.
- Warm standby needs not only instance warmness (artifacts, caches) but also network priming: connections to KV stores, warmed local caches, and pre-populated prefix/KV caches for common contexts (e.g., small prompts).
- Control-plane readiness (ability to change GSLB weights from console/CLI) must be accessible to on-call with a tested access workflow (MFA, emergency role).

Proposed runbook (draft):
Pre-incident prep (warm-standby checklist):
- Keep minimal warm pools in target standby regions: at least 20% of avg RPS sustained by customers pinned to region; auto-scale ramp policy disabled by default so we can estimate capacity.
- Nightly smoke: lightweight synthetic requests (10 qps for 2 minutes) from our synthetic-agent to each warm-standby region to prime caches. Log results to obs-runbook-synthetic.
- Configuration sync: ensure model artifacts and quantized weights are staged and checkedums verified. Command: sha256sum /srv/models/* | grep <model-version>.
- Health hooks: make sure health-check endpoints /_health/region-ready return: {"cacheHits": >= 200, "kvConnections": ok}. (Implementation detail: tiny wrapper script that aggregates).
- BGP/Network probes: maintain a list of 3 external vantage points that query each region for route health (github: traffic-router/infra/probes).

During a region-level degradation (on-call steps):
1) Triage and scope (0-5 min):
   - Confirm alerts: per-route latency spike, instance-level OOMs, or provider notices. Check obs dashboard: regional L7 latency, 95th tail, error rate.
   - Verify provider status pages / Slack provider incident channel.
   - Communicate to #incidents channel with short statement: region, severity, immediate impact, OOO contact.
2) Decide failover strategy (5-12 min):
   - Soft-fail (traffic shift weights) vs Hard-fail (DNS-level failover + BGP adjustments). Default: soft-fail first.
   - If soft-fail: increment fallback region weight in traffic-router by 10% every 30s for first 3 steps, then 20% steps until 100%. Use CLI: traffic-router set-weight --route <route> --region eu-central --weight 10 --dry-run=false.
   - If hard-fail (control-plane unavailable or severe widespread outage): escalate to run emergency BGP change with network team. NOTE: this is rare and requires NOC + on-call director signoff.
3) Verify progress (throughout):
   - Observe both client-side and server-side metrics: active connections by region, per-route CPU utilization, token-per-second breakdown. Watch for queueing and long tails.
   - Validate user-facing: sample a few customer accounts (internal cheat sheet) and run functional tests (end-to-end) via curl to different region endpoints and through GSLB.
4) Post-shift sanity rollback plan (immediate):
   - If any fidelity/regression increase (quality drop for production prompts) above alert threshold, reduce traffic by 20% back towards source region and investigate model variant mismatch.
   - Use traffic-router rollback: traffic-router set-weight --route <route> --region eu-west --weight 80 --force.

DNS specifics / TTL guidance:
- Current: most canonical records TTL = 60s. Observed: many resolvers and ISPs ignore low TTL and cache 2-5x longer. Practical impact: expect 2-6 minutes of residual queries to original region in most cases.
- Recommendation: For critical routes, use shorter TTL (30s) during maintenance windows, but do not rely on <60s for emergency. Instead, pair DNS with GSLB health checks and per-client affinity adjustments via cookies/edge metadata.
- Cloudflare/Edge CDN: purge patterns for route-specific edge caches when shifting; implement a soft-purge that marks responses stale and signals revalidation instead of full purge to avoid cache stampede.

Warm-standby priming details:
- Model layer: pre-load tokenizer and small KV cache for top-100 prompt prefixes. Script: /scripts/prime-prefixes --model <id> --prefix-file top100.txt. Schedule daily at 02:00 UTC.
- Data plane connections: persistent connections to primary datastore must be pre-authenticated. Rotate keys ahead of time and validate IAM roles.
- Autoscaler notes: temporary override flag s2s.force-scale can be used by SRE to set desired capacity for 15m blocks. Do not keep override longer than 60 minutes without leadership approval.

Observability checklist to run after shift:
- Check distribution of new requests by client IP region (should match weight target ±10%).
- Token/unit cost per region vs baseline. Watch for sudden cost spikes due to inefficient batching after shift.
- Error regression: reconstructed eval suite (10 canonical prompts) run against both old and new region variants; capture spurious hallucinations or latency regressions.

Command cheat-sheet (examples):
- traffic-router CLI: traffic-router set-weight --route api.text.generate --region us-west --weight 50
- Route53 change (emergency, guarded): aws route53 change-resource-record-sets --hosted-zone-id Z123 --change-batch file://change.json
- Health checks: curl -sS https://eu-central-api.redwood.internal/_health | jq .
- Synthetic probe run: ./scripts/synthetic-run --region eu-west --profile smoke

Open questions / TODOs (prioritized):
- (P0) Decide canonical TTL policy for production vs maintenance vs emergency. Who signs off? Product + legal?
- (P1) Build UI for one-click rollback that executes a guarded sequence: set-weights -> run smoke tests -> wait -> commit. Add MFA gate for routing-critical routes.
- (P2) Improve warm-standby priming for prefix/KV caches: join with serving-runtime team to surface an API endpoint that returns top prefixes per model version.
- (P2) Document per-customer affinity implications when traffic shifts across regions (GDPR/data residency concerns). Loop in security/compliance.
- (P3) Add unit-economics alerts: if cost/token increases > 25% post-shift for > 10 minutes, page SRE and alert finance.

Notes to self / scribbles: 
- We had forgotten provider TR that re-routes at BGP level; need a diagram of overlays. Add to confluence: /internal/infra/gslb-arch.
- During 10/30 incident, Cloudflare edge delayed by ISP caches. Consider adding a stale-while-revalidate header to 503 responses to signal faster failover semantics.

Action items (owners & ETA):
- Marcus: prototype one-click guarded-shift UI mock (wireframe + API contract), due 2026-03-10.
- Rina: add warm-prime job that pulls top-100 prefixes and exercises them; implement dry-run logs. Due 2026-02-13 (in progress).
- Ava: draft RFC for TTL policy and emergency routing play (link back to CONFLUENCE-1234). Due 2026-03-05.

Appendix: short postmortem sketch (for 2025-10-30 eu-west):
- Incident timeline (approx): 00:00 detect provider BGP flap -> 00:01 on-call paged -> 00:03 synthetic probes show region unreachable from 2 vantage points -> 00:07 attempted weight shift but CDN cache persisted -> 00:11 manual GSLB override + soft-purge -> 00:15 visible recovery for most customers -> 00:34 final normalization as ISP caches TTL expired.
- Root cause: provider-level BGP flap combined with optimistic DNS TTL expectations and missing edge revalidation header.
- Short-term fix: manual escalation path + synthetic probe coverage.
- Long-term fix: TTL policy + UI + warm-priming and CDN behavior changes.

If you are reading this during an active incident: treat this as guidance, not a strict checklist. Call the SRE lead if any step is unclear. Document any deviations in the incident log (SRE-4321).

---
End of draft.
